title: Exploring data with summaries and charts
subtitle: Before modelling, look: the right chart answers a question in a glance.

eda.title: Exploratory data analysis
eda.body: EDA means summarising and plotting data to find its shape, oddities and relationships before modelling. Start univariate (one variable), then bivariate (pairs), then multivariate.

summ.title: Summary statistics
summ.body: Centre: mean, median. Spread: standard deviation, IQR. Shape: skewness. For categories: counts and proportions. Group summaries (mean income by region) are the most common first insight — “group by, then aggregate”.
summ.steps: Sales (k): North 10, 12, 14; South 20, 22. Group means: 12 and 21.

chart.title: Choosing a chart
chart.body:
QuestionChart
Distribution of one numberhistogram / box plot
Compare categoriesbar chart
Change over timeline chart
Relationship of two numbersscatter plot
Part of a wholebar (pie only for few parts)

corr.title: Relationships
corr.body: A scatter plot shows direction, strength and curvature; the correlation r summarises only the linear part. For the sample data r = 0.9 and R² = 0.81. A correlation matrix (heat map) scans many pairs at once.

mislead.title: Honest charts
mislead.body: Start bar charts at zero; keep scales comparable; label axes and units; do not use 3-D effects; show the sample size. Simpson’s paradox: a trend in every group can reverse when groups are pooled — so check subgroups.
mislead.steps: Treatment A cures 81/87 (93 %) of small stones and 192/263 (73 %) of large; B: 234/270 (87 %) and 55/80 (69 %). A wins in both groups, yet pooled A = 273/350 = 78 % and B = 289/350 = 83 %: the mix of stone sizes reverses the ranking.

story.title: Telling the story
story.body: A finding is useful only if the audience acts on it. Lead with the conclusion, show one chart per message, state uncertainty, and note the limits (sample, period, missing data).
